title: City Skyline Outline
statement:
Each building is a rectangle standing on the ground, given as [left, right, height]: it covers every x from left up to (but not including) right. Buildings can overlap, and they may come in any order.

Seen from far away, the buildings merge into one outline. Describe that outline as a list of key points [x, h], sorted by x: at each key point the outline's height changes to h. The last key point is where the last building ends, with height 0.

Two consecutive key points must never have the same height: if the height does not change at some x, there is no key point there.

examples.why: The first building ends at 4, but it is hidden behind the 5, so nothing changes there.
The roofs line up at x = 3 with the same height, so there is no key point at 3.
When the 8 ends at 5, the outline drops to the tallest building still standing, 6, not to 4 or 0.

hints: The outline can only change at a building's left or right edge. If you knew the tallest building covering each such x, you would be done.
Sweep the edges from left to right and keep the set of buildings that currently cover x. You need its maximum height, quickly, while buildings come and go.

A max-heap of (height, right edge). At each x, push every building starting at x, then pop from the top while the top's right edge is ≤ x. The top is the current height (0 if empty). Emit a point when it differs from the last emitted height.

explain.intuition:
The outline only changes where some building starts or ends, so those x values are the only candidates. At each candidate, the height is the tallest building that covers it. The whole problem is keeping "tallest active building" up to date while sweeping left to right.

A max-heap gives the tallest one, but removing an arbitrary building from a heap is slow. The trick is lazy removal: store each building with its right edge, and only throw out buildings when they reach the top. A building buried under a taller one can stay in the heap after it has ended, because it doesn't affect the maximum until it surfaces, and then it gets popped.
steps: Collect every left and right edge, sort them and remove duplicates. Sort buildings by left edge.
For each edge x: push every building with left == x as (height, right) onto a max-heap.
Pop while the top building's right ≤ x: it has ended.
The current height is the top's height, or 0 if the heap is empty.
If it differs from the last emitted height, append [x, height].
pitfalls: Emitting a point at every edge. Hidden ends (the 3 ending at 4 in example 1) and touching equal roofs (example 2) must not produce points.
Handling ends before starts at the same x as separate events, which briefly drops to a lower height and emits two points at one x.
Dropping to 0 when the tallest building ends instead of to the next tallest one still standing.

solutions.title: Check every edge against every building
solutions.idea: For each distinct edge x, scan all buildings to find the tallest one covering x, and emit a point when the height changes.

solutions.title: Sweep with a max-heap and lazy removal
solutions.idea: Sweep the edges left to right. A max-heap of (height, right) holds the active buildings; expired ones are popped only when they reach the top.

followups: Solve it by divide and conquer: compute the outlines of each half and merge them like two sorted lists.
Buildings arrive one at a time and you must update the outline after each. Which structure replaces the heap?
